metadata.title: PISA 2022 Results (Volume IV): How Financially Smart Are Students?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This volume reports results from the OECD PISA 2022 assessment, which is implemented using a complex, multi-stage sampling design of students within schools and schools within participating education systems. The report indicates that PISA 2022 collected data from nearly 700 000 students across 81 OECD Member and partner economies, and that an optional financial literacy assessment was administered to about 100 000 students across 20 participating economies. For analyses of PISA achievement and financial literacy outcomes, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights (and, where provided, replicate weights) supplied with the PISA microdata to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex design. This excerpt does not specify the exact weight variable names or whether replicate-weight procedures were used in the reported analyses, so the precise weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The provided text is a high-level OECD results volume describing PISA 2022 and summarising patterns (e.g., score changes, shares of low performers) rather than documenting an empirical model that uses PV-based cognitive achievement as an explicit dependent variable. Because the excerpt does not report the PV estimation/combining procedure or any missing-data strategy for an ML/statistical model, the PV and missing-data handling details are not available in the supplied material. This is therefore a reporting gap for methodological specifics, not evidence that PVs or missing-data procedures were absent in the underlying PISA technical production.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 student data from participating OECD Member and partner economies; the excerpt also notes that the financial literacy assessment was optional and administered to a subset of about 100 000 students from 20 participating economies. No further analytic filtering criteria (e.g., grade restrictions beyond PISA’s target age group, exclusions, or completion thresholds) are specified in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume summarises PISA 2022 results, including a dedicated focus on financial literacy (Volume IV). PISA 2022 is administered to 15-year-old students and, in 2022, nearly 700 000 students from 81 OECD Member and partner economies participated in the main PISA assessment, while an optional financial literacy assessment was taken by nearly 100 000 students from 20 economies. The report describes broad achievement patterns (e.g., average declines in reading and mathematics compared with 2018) and interprets them alongside contextual factors such as school closures, remote learning, technology use, teacher support, and parental engagement. It also frames financial literacy as a life skill and reports that socio-economically disadvantaged students are over-represented among low performers in financial literacy, motivating policy action to prevent widening inequalities. The excerpt does not provide the technical modelling details (e.g., PV combining rules, missing-data handling, or any ML model evaluation), so the methodological basis for the reported score comparisons cannot be verified from this text alone.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA results volume (Volume IV) that provides descriptive and interpretive reporting of assessment outcomes rather than an empirical ML study with a documented predictive pipeline. The excerpt does not include the technical methods section needed to extract PV handling, missing-data procedures, model specifications, or per-target predictive metrics, so the schema fields for ML techniques and main findings are intentionally left empty. The provided text is therefore insufficient to support extraction of student-level modelling results, but it is sufficient to identify the assessment context (PISA 2022 and the optional financial literacy component) and high-level outcome patterns.
